title: Checkpoint: Mind and Consciousness
objective: After this level you can compare dualism, physicalism and functionalism and say which puzzle about consciousness each struggles with.
summary: Dualism, the identity theory and functionalism each answer the mind-body problem and meet their own objection, while Nagel, Jackson and Chalmers challenge physical theories of consciousness.

cards.headline: Chapter 4 finale: one problem, three theories, one stubborn puzzle.
cards.body: How does a mind fit into a physical world? Line up the answers, the objection that dogs each one, and the puzzle that troubles the physical ones.

cards.headline: Three theories and their weak spots

items.label: Dualism
points: Descartes: a thinking mind with no extension, distinct from the body
Elisabeth: how could it ever move a body?

items.label: Identity theory
points: Each mental state just is a brain state
Putnam: octopuses seem to feel pain with very different brains

items.label: Functionalism
points: A mental state is whatever plays the right role
Block: a nation playing those roles might feel nothing

cards.headline: The puzzle for physical theories
cards.body: The identity theory is a form of physicalism, and functionalism fits with it too, though it lets minds run on things other than brains. Consciousness is the shared worry. Nagel argued that experience is tied to a point of view a physical theory leaves out. Jackson’s Mary seemed to learn something no physical fact contained. Chalmers argued that explaining every function leaves the hard problem standing.

cards.headline: Still an open question
cards.body: Where do professional philosophers stand? In a 2020 survey, 51% accepted or leaned toward materialism about the mind, and 22% toward dualism. A majority, but no consensus: the debate is very much alive.

cards.headline: Chapter 4 complete
learned: How dualism, the identity theory and functionalism each answer the mind-body problem.
Why Elisabeth, Putnam and Block each found a weak spot in one of those theories.
What Nagel’s bat, Mary’s room and the hard problem say physical facts might leave out.
What Turing’s imitation game tests, and why Searle thought passing it isn’t understanding.

questions.prompt: Mind and Consciousness recap: what did Princess Elisabeth ask Descartes in 1643?

options.label: Whether animals have minds and souls like ours
options.rationale: Her question was about mind and body.

options.label: Whether the Earth moves around the Sun
options.rationale: Her question was about mind and body.

options.label: How a soul that is only a thinking thing can move a body
How to prove that God exists
options.rationale: Her question was about mind and body.

questions.explanation: Elisabeth asked how a thinking, unextended soul could move the body to produce voluntary actions.

questions.prompt: Mind and Consciousness recap: on the ability hypothesis, what does Mary gain when she first sees red?

options.label: A new physical fact about wavelengths
options.rationale: She already had all the physical facts.

options.label: Abilities to imagine, remember and recognize red
Nothing whatsoever
options.rationale: The reply grants she gains something.

options.label: Proof that dualism is true
options.rationale: The reply is meant to defend physicalism.

questions.explanation: Lewis and Nemirow say Mary gains know-how, a bundle of abilities, not a new fact.

questions.prompt: In Mind and Consciousness, which objection is paired with the identity theory?

options.label: A nation playing brain roles might feel nothing
A mind with no extension can’t push a body
Octopuses seem to feel pain with very different brains
The visitor who can’t find the University

questions.explanation: Putnam argued that pain can’t be one kind of brain state if creatures with very different brains all feel it.

questions.prompt: In Mind and Consciousness, which puzzles challenge physical theories of the mind in general, not just one of them?

options.label: Nagel’s bat, Mary’s room and the hard problem
Galileo’s tied balls and Gyges’s ring
options.rationale: Those come from Level 3, on other topics.

options.label: The ship of fools and the lottery
Elisabeth’s letter alone

questions.explanation: All three press the worry that physical facts may leave out what experience is like.

questions.prompt: Mind and Consciousness recap: which theory most easily lets a silicon android feel pain, and why?

options.label: Dualism, because androids have souls
options.rationale: Dualism says nothing about androids’ souls.

options.label: The identity theory, because pain is always C-fiber firing
options.rationale: That would rule the android out.

options.label: Idealism, because matter is mental
options.rationale: Idealism wasn’t one of the compared theories.

options.label: Functionalism, because any state playing pain’s role counts as pain

questions.explanation: Functionalism defines pain by its role, so a silicon state playing that role counts.
